analysis.one_liner: Postponed enforcement of new truck driver sleeper-berth rest rules for three months.
analysis.headline: The House never voted: the bill sat in a Transportation subcommittee until the Congress ended, so the new rest rules were enforced on schedule.
analysis.plain_summary: In August 2005, the federal truck safety agency issued new rules governing how long-haul truck drivers split their rest time while sleeping in the cab's sleeper berth, with enforcement starting October 1, 2005. This bill would have let the old rules stay in force until January 1, 2006, so trucking companies and drivers would have three more months to retrain and adjust schedules without facing fines. The bill was referred to a House subcommittee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, motor carriers and their drivers would have been spared fines, citations, and out-of-service violations while they retrained drivers and adjusted pickup and delivery schedules for the new rule; the bill's own findings state the industry said it could not complete retraining before the October 1 enforcement date.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have kept the pre-2004 hours-of-service rules and compatible state laws in force until January 1, 2006, replacing enforcement of the new FMCSA sleeper-berth rule during that window.

Its findings argue that subjecting drivers and carriers to fines and citations before they had time to understand and comply with the new rule would be unwise, and that a three-month enforcement delay would provide a reasonable compliance period.

The bill notes that while the safety agency had issued 'soft enforcement' guidance, state enforcement officials were not bound by it and could fully enforce the new rule starting October 1, 2005; the bill would have bound that enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Enforcement of a fatigue-related trucking safety rule would have been pushed back three months, a cost borne by the traveling public in the form of continued operation under older rest rules; the bill's subjects include traffic accidents and safety.

drawbacks.text: Delaying enforcement of hours-of-service rules means drivers would have operated under older rest rules for another three months, postponing whatever safety benefit the new rule provided; the bill's own subject list includes traffic accidents and safety, and the new rule governs driver rest periods.

The bill acknowledges the new rule was 'scheduled to become effective and fully enforceable by State officials on October 1, 2005,' so the delay was a relief granted to an industry after the compliance date had already been set, which weakens the predictability of safety-rule deadlines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was narrow and one-time: three months of compliance relief from fines for carriers and drivers adjusting to a changed sleeper-berth rule. The cost was a brief postponement of enforcing a rest-rule aimed at fatigue-related crashes. As a short transition measure the trade-off is defensible, but it is a small bill whose main constituency was the trucking industry, and the House never even considered it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then passed to its Highways subcommittee, and no committee or floor action ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young introduced the bill on September 29, 2005, for himself and 13 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
The next day, September 30, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways, Transit and Pipelines.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or Senate consideration before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

The bill's substance was a three-month enforcement delay: the new FMCSA sleeper-berth rule would have become enforceable on January 1, 2006, with the January 4, 2004 rules remaining in force in the meantime.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the new sleeper-berth rule's enforcement proceeded as scheduled rather than being pushed back for the industry, so the main beneficiaries of the outcome were the rule as written and, indirectly, road safety; trucking companies lost their requested three-month grace period. That said, this was a modest measure, and nothing dramatic changed for anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Safety rule took effect on schedule

for.name: Don Young
for.role: Chairman, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 29, 2005, with 13 original cosponsors including both parties.

for.name: 7 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Peter DeFazio, an original cosponsor.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Highways, Transit and Pipelines
against.role: Referral panel, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 30, 2005, and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew 52 cosponsors, 45 Republicans and 7 Democrats, so support leaned heavily Republican but was not purely partisan; the decisive fact is that it never moved past subcommittee referral in either direction.

industries.note: The bill would have spared carriers three months of fines, citations, and scheduling changes while they adapted to the new rest rule, per its own findings. Their gain came from postponing enforcement of a fatigue-safety regulation, which runs against the public's interest in enforced rest rules.

Drivers would have been protected from out-of-service violations and fines during the transition, but they would also have operated under older, less restrictive rest rules for three more months. The bill's findings frame the delay as protecting drivers from penalties for rules they had not been trained on.
